evidence: createApp registers Express routes and passes each one straight to FulfilmentService methods (listProducts, getProduct, addProduct, placeOrder, listOrders, getOrder, transition, cancelOrder).
The POST /orders and POST /products handlers only check the structure and types of the request body (typeof checks), which is input validation at the transport boundary.
GET /orders uses the domain's isOrderState instead of copying the state rules into this file.
The STATUS map and the error middleware turn DomainError.kind and SyntaxError into HTTP status codes, which is an HTTP adapter concern.
The transitions array only lists route endpoints; whether a transition is allowed is decided by service.transition.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The file passes. src/infrastructure/http-app.ts is an Express HTTP adapter, and everything it does is transport work that fits the infrastructure layer: setting up routes, reading request parameters, checking the shape of JSON request bodies, mapping results to responses, and turning errors into HTTP status codes. The real business work is handed to FulfilmentService (placeOrder, transition, cancelOrder, addProduct). This includes stock handling, order state transitions and cancellation rules. Checking whether the order state is valid is done by the domain's isOrderState, not rewritten here. The typeof checks on request bodies only check that the input has the right structure at the HTTP boundary. They don't encode business invariants. The loop over the transitions ["pay","pack","ship","deliver"] only lists the route names. Which transitions are actually allowed is still decided by service.transition. I found no persistence and no business rules in this file.
